 November 1, 2026 
 COMMUNITY NEWS 
 By Fraser Sherman 
 Correspondent
 ORANGE COUNTY – Changes to the federal SNAP program could cost Orange County an extra $2 million a year to fight local hunger and food insecurity. Or possibly much less: one challenge to the county budget is that the amount isn’t predictable.
 “You’re going to see some volatility,” Assistant County Manager Kirk Vaughn told the County Commission at its Oct. 20 informational meeting. If the new policies had taken effect in 2023, Orange County’s cost over the past four years would have ranged from under $300,000 to over $2 million.
 What H.R. 1 has changed 
 When H.R. 1 became law in 2025, it affected tax rates, tax deductions, Medicaid eligibility and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). Once known as the Food Stamp program, SNAP provides benefits to help recipients buy food. In a joint presentation, Vaughn and Social Services Director Lindsey Shewmaker broke down the changes to SNAP benefits:
 Able-bodied adults 55 and older are no longer exempt from the program’s work requirements. The exemption doesn’t kick in until 65.
 Parents lose their work exemption when their kids turn 14, rather than 18.
 H.R. 1 eliminates the exemptions from work requirements formerly granted to veterans, the homeless and young people aging out of foster care.
 Fewer noncitizens can qualify for SNAP.
 People covered by the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, which helps with heating and cooling costs, may receive lower SNAP benefits.
 H.R. 1 also changes the funding formula. The federal government used to cover 50% of administrative costs; under H.R. 1, North Carolina and other states must pay 75%.
 “Spoiler alert,” Shewmaker said, “the state has decided to push that cost to the county.” As the new rules took effect partway through 2026, they cost Orange County $900,000 this year. Next fiscal year it’ll be $1.2 million.
 Starting next year, states that have error rates higher than 6 percent of their caseload — errors where recipients receive too much or too little in benefits — will also have to pay a greater share of the cost of benefits. In North Carolina, local governments also bear that cost.
 Food insecurity 
 Orange County estimates 13 percent of residents live with food insecurity. Food security is the certainty that you can get safe, healthy food when you want it; food insecurity hits when someone lacks that certainty. Even before H.R. 1, half of the county’s food-insecure residents made too much to qualify for SNAP. The new eligibility restrictions will remove more people from the program.
 In June 2026, Orange County had 4,300 households—roughly 8,000 participants—receiving Food and Nutrition Services (FNS), the official state name for SNAP. That’s despite an 87 percent decline in the SNAP caseload since July of last year.
 Shewmaker said the changes will affect more than SNAP recipients: the program’s benefit payments put $31 million into the local economy. That’s especially important in rural areas where grocery stores rely on SNAP for a large share of their revenue. “That’s a huge economic incentive that’s lost.”
 The Associated Press says tougher SNAP eligibility requirements led to 4.3 million fewer people using the program in 2026. In North Carolina, Shewmaker said SNAP use is down 12 percent and still decreasing. “The assumption is people are still needing it.”
 While caseloads are shrinking, Shewmaker added, the amount of administrative work involved has increased. Under H.R. 1, the program requires additional hearings, increased notification and extra verification. Orange County also has to track the expanded work requirement and review more cases.
 The high cost of mistakes 
 Currently, the federal government pays 100 percent of SNAP benefits. If North Carolina’s error rate is above 6 percent, Orange County will have to cover part of that cost. The state payment formula will assign Orange County, like other affected local governments, a share of the state’s costs, rather than basing it on the county’s error rate.
 Shewmaker and Vaughn said the problem is less about fraud and more about staff mistakes, clients who don’t understand the complicated reporting, or people in the gig economy who lose track of a payment. The error rate and county costs can vary year to year: over the past four years, if current policies had applied, Orange County would have had to pay $282,165, $2.1 million, $795,772 and $1.29 million. In the future, the state won’t complete calculations for a given year until after the county has passed its budget.
 North Carolina is working to get its current rate, 6.9 percent, down below the cutoff. Shewmaker said she doesn’t think they’d get there in time to avoid a penalty for the next fiscal year. Orange County, like other affected governments, will be forced to find the money somewhere.
 What next? 
 “I don’t think the transfer to local government was expected,” Shewmaker said, since no other state has shifted costs this way. She’s been meeting with state and federal senators to explain the impact. Even delaying the new rules for a year or two might buy enough time for combined state and local government efforts to lower the error rate.
 Steps to reduce errors include updating technology, identifying high-risk cases and improving quality control. They also include training interviewers to ask awkward, invasive questions about income and self-employment that clients, even if they’re not hiding anything, may resent.
 County Commission Chair Jean Hamilton said that while few people attended the Oct. 20 meeting, “folks will have plenty to say at budget time when cuts must be made.” The board must consider trade-offs and compromises ahead of time and communicate clearly with county residents.
 Commissioner Rani Dasi said the board must also consider people squeezed out of SNAP by new policies, such as work requirements that apply up to age 65. “We can’t let these people fall away.” Hopefully residents will support spending tax dollars on people “in their worst time of need.”
 You can watch the meeting here .
 Fraser Sherman has worked for newspapers, including the Destin Log, the Pensacola News-Journal and the Raleigh Public Record. Born in England, he’d still live in Florida if he hadn’t met the perfect woman and moved to Durham to marry her. He’s the author of several film reference books and has published one novel and several short story collections. This reporter can be reached at: Information@TheLocalReporter.press
